headline: Highest risk is data leakage and cascading error: RD-Agent’s API/log handling can expose sensitive research data while Airflow’s broad egress can propagate it downstream.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Airflow has no browser and no documented shared channel to RD-Agent, so direct prompt injection is not evident. However, RD-Agent can run browsers and write logs, and Airflow can call APIs with broad egress; if operators manually pass outputs between them, injected content could ride along. This is a weak, operator-mediated pathway, so low is appropriate.
conditions: IF operators manually copy RD-Agent outputs into Airflow task definitions or prompts, injection becomes plausible.
IF a shared file or clipboard bridge is introduced between the agents, untrusted content can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Disable manual copy-paste of generated text into prompts.
Require human review before any RD-Agent output is reused in Airflow.
Use a strict template for any transferred text.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for transferred artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: RD-Agent explicitly touches financial reports, competition datasets, execution traces, logs, and secrets, while Airflow has broad network egress and API-calling surfaces. Even without a shared filesystem, pairing them can move sensitive data from RD-Agent into Airflow-managed workflows or external APIs. The interaction is plausible in default deployments, but the profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so medium fits.
conditions: IF RD-Agent processes any of the listed sensitive data classes and Airflow ingests its outputs, leakage risk is present.
IF Airflow tasks forward RD-Agent artifacts to third-party APIs, those contents may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Restrict RD-Agent inputs to non-sensitive samples.
Block Airflow tasks from sending RD-Agent artifacts to external APIs.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately after testing.
Store RD-Agent logs in a separate, access-controlled directory.
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss-prevention checks on inter-agent transfers.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have broad network egress, and RD-Agent supports multiple instances plus Docker isolation, while Airflow is a data orchestrator that commonly coordinates mutable workflows. The profiles do not show a shared writable directory or git state, so high is not justified. Still, overlapping mutable workflow control and external API use can conflict in default operations, making medium the safer choice under uncertainty.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same downstream resource without locking, conflicts can occur.
IF Airflow orchestrates RD-Agent runs concurrently, duplicate or out-of-order updates may happen.
mitigations: Serialize any shared downstream writes.
Assign separate service accounts per agent.
Use unique output paths per run.
Check for duplicate jobs before launching a second run.
requires-engineering: add distributed locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Airflow is an automation orchestrator, so if it consumes RD-Agent outputs as task inputs, it may act on unverified research claims or logs. RD-Agent’s research-oriented outputs and Airflow’s execution role create a plausible cascade from analysis to action. The profiles do not prove automatic trust, so medium is appropriate rather than high.
conditions: IF Airflow uses RD-Agent outputs as authoritative inputs, downstream tasks may execute incorrect actions.
IF RD-Agent emits malformed or stale results and Airflow lacks validation, errors can cascade.
mitigations: Add a validation step before Airflow consumes RD-Agent outputs.
Require schema checks on all transferred artifacts.
Compare RD-Agent results against a second source for critical tasks.
Limit Airflow actions to dry-run mode first.
requires-engineering: implement automated verification gates between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: RD-Agent explicitly handles financial reports, competition datasets, execution traces, logs, and secrets, while Airflow has broad egress and API calls. That creates a plausible compliance mismatch if regulated or confidential data flows through Airflow to external services. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, so the risk is medium, not high.
conditions: IF regulated data such as financial reports or secrets is processed by RD-Agent and then sent through Airflow to external APIs, compliance obligations may be triggered.
IF retention or residency requirements apply to RD-Agent logs, Airflow forwarding them can violate policy.
mitigations: Classify data before passing it between agents.
Keep regulated datasets out of Airflow-connected runs.
Disable external API calls for compliance-sensitive jobs.
Review retention settings for logs and artifacts.
requires-engineering: document residency and DPA boundaries for both systems.
